claim: Mutations in the X-linked ZDHHC9 gene cause cognitive deficits in humans.
source: Mutations in the X-linked ZDHHC9 gene cause cognitive deficits in humans, with a subset of patients suffering from epilepsy.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on ZDHHC9 mutations and XLID

claim: A subset of patients with ZDHHC9 mutations suffer from epilepsy.
source: Mutations in the X-linked ZDHHC9 gene cause cognitive deficits in humans, with a subset of patients suffering from epilepsy.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Expression of human and mouse ZDHHC9 orthologs is far higher in myelinating oligodendrocytes than in other CNS cell types.
source: X-linked intellectual disability (XLID) is often ascribed to neuronal deficits, but here we report that expression of human and mouse ZDHHC9 orthologs is far higher in myelinating oligodendrocytes (OLs) than in other CNS cell types.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1

claim: ZDHHC9 is the most highly expressed PAT in oligodendrocytes.
source: ZDHHC9 codes for a protein acyltransferase (PAT), and we found that ZDHHC9 is the most highly expressed PAT in OLs.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq FPKM values shown in Figure 1C

claim: Wild-type ZDHHC9 localizes to Golgi outposts in oligodendrocyte processes.
source: Wild-type ZDHHC9 localizes to Golgi outposts in OL processes, but other PATs and XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 are restricted to OL cell bodies.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Other PATs are restricted to oligodendrocyte cell bodies.
source: Wild-type ZDHHC9 localizes to Golgi outposts in OL processes, but other PATs and XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 are restricted to OL cell bodies.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2

claim: XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 are restricted to oligodendrocyte cell bodies.
source: Wild-type ZDHHC9 localizes to Golgi outposts in OL processes, but other PATs and XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 are restricted to OL cell bodies.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C and D

claim: Mice lacking Zdhhc9 have grossly normal oligodendrocyte development.
source: Using genetic tools for OL progenitor fate tracing and sparse cell labeling, we show that mice lacking Zdhhc9 have grossly normal OL development but display extensive morphological and structural myelin abnormalities.
evidence: Supported by OL quantification data in Figure 3

claim: Mice lacking Zdhhc9 display extensive morphological and structural myelin abnormalities.
source: Using genetic tools for OL progenitor fate tracing and sparse cell labeling, we show that mice lacking Zdhhc9 have grossly normal OL development but display extensive morphological and structural myelin abnormalities.
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis in Figures 4-6

claim: Acute Zdhhc9 knockdown in cultured conditions broadly phenocopies the deficits seen in Zdhhc9 knockout mice.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that these deficits are OL-autonomous, they are broadly phenocopied by acute Zdhhc9 knockdown in cultured conditions.
evidence: Supported by cultured OL data in Figure 7

claim: ZDHHC9 palmitoylates Myelin Basic Protein (MBP) in heterologous cells.
source: Finally, we found that ZDHHC9 palmitoylates Myelin Basic Protein (MBP) in heterologous cells, and that palmitoylation of MBP is impaired in the Zdhhc9 knockout brain.
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8A and B

claim: Palmitoylation of MBP is impaired in the Zdhhc9 knockout brain.
source: Finally, we found that ZDHHC9 palmitoylates Myelin Basic Protein (MBP) in heterologous cells, and that palmitoylation of MBP is impaired in the Zdhhc9 knockout brain.
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data from brain tissue in Figure 8C and D

claim: ZDHHC9-associated XLID mutations include nonsense mutations, missense mutations affecting key amino acids, splice site mutations, insertions, and deletions that result in frameshifts.
source: XLID-associated ZDHHC9 mutations include nonsense mutations and missense mutations affecting key amino acids, as well as splice site mutations, insertions, and deletions that result in frameshifts.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on ZDHHC9 mutations

claim: All ZDHHC9 XLID-associated genetic changes are predicted to be loss-of-function.
source: Importantly, all these genetic changes are predicted to be loss-of-function.
evidence: Based on inference from the types of mutations described

claim: ZDHHC9 is essential for higher brain function.
source: These findings suggest that ZDHHC9 is essential for higher brain function.
evidence: Inferred from the loss-of-function mutations causing intellectual disability

claim: Many XLID genes are neuronally enriched.
source: Given that many XLID genes are neuronally enriched (Devys et al., 1993; Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Toya et al., 2023; Rusconi et al., 2008; Guarnieri et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2006; Bienvenu et al., 2002), an a priori hypothesis is that ZDHHC9 acts in neurons.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Patients with ZDHHC9 mutations have grossly normal gray matter.
source: However, patients with ZDHHC9 mutations have grossly normal gray matter (GM) but reduced brain white matter (WM) volume, especially in the corpus callosum (CC) (Baker et al., 2015; Raymond et al., 2007; Masurel-Paulet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies

claim: Patients with ZDHHC9 mutations have reduced brain white matter volume, especially in the corpus callosum.
source: However, patients with ZDHHC9 mutations have grossly normal gray matter (GM) but reduced brain white matter (WM) volume, especially in the corpus callosum (CC) (Baker et al., 2015; Raymond et al., 2007; Masurel-Paulet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies

claim: ZDHHC9 mutations are linked to cerebral palsy.
source: ZDHHC9 mutations are also linked to cerebral palsy, a condition in which intellectual disability is often associated with WM impairment (WMI) (Jiang et al., 2019; Odding et al., 2006; van Eyk et al., 2019; McMichael et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: In cerebral palsy, intellectual disability is often associated with white matter impairment.
source: ZDHHC9 mutations are also linked to cerebral palsy, a condition in which intellectual disability is often associated with WM impairment (WMI) (Jiang et al., 2019; Odding et al., 2006; van Eyk et al., 2019; McMichael et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Zdhhc9 knockout mice exhibit white matter volume reductions.
source: Notably, Zdhhc9 knockout (KO) mice exhibit WM volume reductions and seizure-like activity (Kouskou et al., 2018; Shimell et al., 2019), as well as behavioral phenotypes seen in other mouse models of ID (Kouskou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Zdhhc9 knockout mice exhibit seizure-like activity.
source: Notably, Zdhhc9 knockout (KO) mice exhibit WM volume reductions and seizure-like activity (Kouskou et al., 2018; Shimell et al., 2019), as well as behavioral phenotypes seen in other mouse models of ID (Kouskou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Zdhhc9 knockout mice exhibit behavioral phenotypes seen in other mouse models of intellectual disability.
source: Notably, Zdhhc9 knockout (KO) mice exhibit WM volume reductions and seizure-like activity (Kouskou et al., 2018; Shimell et al., 2019), as well as behavioral phenotypes seen in other mouse models of ID (Kouskou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: ZDHHC9 codes for a protein acyltransferase (PAT).
source: ZDHHC9 codes for a protein acyltransferase (PAT), an enzyme that catalyzes the modification of protein cysteine residues with palmitate and related fatty acids.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ZDHHC9 function

claim: Protein acyltransferases catalyze the modification of protein cysteine residues with palmitate and related fatty acids.
source: ZDHHC9 codes for a protein acyltransferase (PAT), an enzyme that catalyzes the modification of protein cysteine residues with palmitate and related fatty acids.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PAT function

claim: Palmitoylation plays a critical role in targeting proteins to specific subcellular membrane locations.
source: This process, termed palmitoylation (also known as S-palmitoylation or S-acylation), plays a critical role in targeting proteins to specific subcellular membrane locations (Linder and Deschenes, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Major myelin proteins in the nervous system, including Proteolipid protein (PLP), Myelin basic protein (MBP), Myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), and Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG), are palmitoylated.
source: Nearly 30 years ago, it was reported that major myelin proteins in the nervous system, including Proteolipid protein (PLP), Myelin basic protein (MBP), Myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), and Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG), are palmitoylated (Bizzozero and Good, 1990; Agrawal et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Proteomic studies revealed many palmitoylated myelin proteins.
source: Later proteomic studies revealed many other palmitoylated myelin proteins (Kang et al., 2008; Wan et al., 2013; Gorenberg et al., 2022; Edmonds et al., 2017), and an isolated study suggested that palmitoylation targets myelin proteins to the plasma membrane of cultured OLs (Schneider et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Palmitoylation targets myelin proteins to the plasma membrane of cultured oligodendrocytes.
source: Later proteomic studies revealed many other palmitoylated myelin proteins (Kang et al., 2008; Wan et al., 2013; Gorenberg et al., 2022; Edmonds et al., 2017), and an isolated study suggested that palmitoylation targets myelin proteins to the plasma membrane of cultured OLs (Schneider et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Little is known regarding how myelin protein palmitoylation is regulated.
source: Despite these findings, little is known regarding how myelin protein palmitoylation is regulated and the functional importance of this process for higher brain function.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of the field

claim: Little is known regarding the functional importance of myelin protein palmitoylation for higher brain function.
source: Despite these findings, little is known regarding how myelin protein palmitoylation is regulated and the functional importance of this process for higher brain function.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of the field

claim: Genes previously known to be highly expressed in myelinating oligodendrocytes were highly enriched in OL-specific RNA preparations from Mobp-EGFP mice.
source: Bioinformatics analysis indicated that genes previously known to be highly expressed in myelinating OLs (McMichael et al., 2015) were highly enriched in our OL-specific RNA preparations (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Expression levels of genes specific to other neural cell types and endothelial cells were very low in OL-specific RNA preparations.
source: In contrast, expression levels of genes specific to other neural cell types and endothelial cells were very low, confirming that our transcriptomic dataset is highly OL-specific (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Zdhhc9 is the most highly expressed PAT in oligodendrocytes with FPKM approximately 180.
source: We found that Zdhhc9 is the most highly expressed PAT in OLs (FPKM ~180), with mRNAs for Zdhhc14, Zdhhc17, and Zdhhc20 present at lower but detectable levels (FPKM 30~70) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by FPKM values shown in Figure 1C

claim: Zdhhc14, Zdhhc17, and Zdhhc20 are present at lower but detectable levels in oligodendrocytes (FPKM 30-70).
source: We found that Zdhhc9 is the most highly expressed PAT in OLs (FPKM ~180), with mRNAs for Zdhhc14, Zdhhc17, and Zdhhc20 present at lower but detectable levels (FPKM 30~70) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by FPKM values shown in Figure 1C

claim: The remaining PATs were expressed at far lower levels (FPKM <10) in oligodendrocytes.
source: The remaining PATs were expressed at far lower levels (FPKM <10).
evidence: Supported by FPKM values from RNA-seq data

claim: ZDHHC9 activity requires a conserved partner, Golgi Complex Protein-16 (gene name Golga7).
source: ZDHHC9 activity requires a conserved partner, Golgi Complex Protein-16 (gene name Golga7) (Shimell et al., 2019; Swarthout et al., 2005; Nguyen et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Golga7 was abundantly expressed in oligodendrocytes, at far higher levels than other Golga family members.
source: We found that Golga7 was also abundantly expressed in OLs, at far higher levels than other Golga family members, including Golga7's closest paralog, Golga7b (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by FPKM values shown in Figure 1D

claim: FPKM values for Zdhhc9 and Golga7 were far lower in total RNA preps obtained from whole cortices without specific cell type isolation.
source: FPKM values for Zdhhc9 and Golga7 were far lower in total RNA preps obtained from whole cortices without specific cell type isolation (Figure 1E, left Heatmap), suggesting that high Zdhhc9 and Golga7 expression is an OL-specific feature, rather than a general characteristic of CNS cells.
evidence: Supported by comparison of FPKM values in Figure 1E

claim: High Zdhhc9 and Golga7 expression is an oligodendrocyte-specific feature, rather than a general characteristic of CNS cells.
source: FPKM values for Zdhhc9 and Golga7 were far lower in total RNA preps obtained from whole cortices without specific cell type isolation (Figure 1E, left Heatmap), suggesting that high Zdhhc9 and Golga7 expression is an OL-specific feature, rather than a general characteristic of CNS cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of FPKM values between OL-specific and whole cortex samples

claim: Another CNS cell type-specific RNA-Seq dataset confirmed high and specific expression of Zdhhc9 and Golga7 in myelin-forming oligodendrocytes.
source: Consistent with this notion, examination of another CNS cell type-specific RNA-Seq dataset, obtained with sorted cells from P17 brain cortices via immunopanning (Zhang et al., 2014), confirmed high and specific expression of Zdhhc9 and Golga7 in myelin-forming OLs (Figure 1E, right Heatmap).
evidence: Supported by data from Zhang et al., 2014 shown in Figure 1E

claim: In human CNS, both ZDHHC9 and GOLGA7 are enriched in oligodendrocytes, compared to any other PATs or other GOLGA family members.
source: Moreover, examination of a human RNA-Seq study (Zhang et al., 2016) revealed that, like mouse CNS, both ZDHHC9 and GOLGA7 are enriched in human OLs, compared to any other PATs or other GOLGA family members, respectively. (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data from Zhang et al., 2016 shown in Figure 1F

claim: HA-ZDHHC3, HA-ZDHHC7, and HA-ZDHHC17 were only detected in oligodendrocyte cell bodies.
source: Under these conditions, HA-ZDHHC3, HA-ZDHHC7, and HA-ZDHHC17 were only detected in OL cell bodies, consistent with their restriction to the somatic Golgi in other cell types (Fang et al., 2006; Niu et al., 2020; Collura et al., 2020; Ohno et al., 2006; Greaves et al., 2008; Figure 2B and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B and D

claim: HA-ZDHHC9 was detected both in oligodendrocyte cell bodies and in discrete puncta in oligodendrocyte processes.
source: In contrast, HA-ZDHHC9 was detected both in OL cell bodies and in discrete puncta in OL processes (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B and D

claim: Within oligodendrocyte cell bodies, ZDHHC9 partially colocalized with the Golgi marker GM130.
source: Within OL cell bodies, ZDHHC9 partially colocalized with the Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: ZDHHC9 colocalized in part with additional Golgi markers (TGN38, Giantin).
source: Consistent with this Golgi localization, ZDHHC9 also colocalized in part with additional Golgi markers (TGN38, Giantin; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: Golgi markers GM130, TGN38, and Giantin were not detected in oligodendrocyte processes.
source: However, these markers were not detected in OL processes and therefore did not colocalize with ZDHHC9 in this latter location (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: XLID-associated HA-ZDHHC9 mutants (R96W, R148W, P150S) did not localize to oligodendrocyte processes.
source: In contrast to HA-ZDHHC9WT, these XLID-associated HA-ZDHHC9 mutants did not localize to OL processes (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C and D

claim: Myc-tagged Golga7 colocalized extensively with HA-ZDHHC9 in both oligodendrocyte cell bodies and in discrete puncta in oligodendrocyte processes.
source: Consistent with this role, myc-tagged Golga7 (myc-Golga7) colocalized extensively with HA-ZDHHC9 in both OL cell bodies and in discrete puncta in OL processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: ZDHHC9-positive puncta in oligodendrocyte processes colocalized with GFP-tagged ManII (ManII-GFP).
source: Consistent with their assignation as Golgi outposts, ZDHHC9-positive puncta in OL processes colocalized with GFP-tagged ManII (ManII-GFP) and, to a lesser extent, with Flag-tagged TPPP (TPPP-Flag) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: ZDHHC9-positive puncta in oligodendrocyte processes colocalized to a lesser extent with Flag-tagged TPPP (TPPP-Flag).
source: Consistent with their assignation as Golgi outposts, ZDHHC9-positive puncta in OL processes colocalized with GFP-tagged ManII (ManII-GFP) and, to a lesser extent, with Flag-tagged TPPP (TPPP-Flag) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: There was no apparent difference in MBP-labeled oligodendrocyte processes between WT control and Zdhhc9 KO mice at 6 weeks of age.
source: Histological observations of brain sections from 6-week-old male mice revealed no apparent difference in MBP-labeled OL processes between WT control and Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A

claim: Oligodendrocyte numbers in cortex and corpus callosum did not differ significantly between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: OL numbers in CTX and the corpus callosum (CC), assessed using OL markers aspartoacylase (ASPA) or Quaking 7 (recognized by antibody CC1), also did not detect any significant difference between the two groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: Preliminary analysis of the early oligodendrocyte marker BCAS1 did not reveal obvious differences between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: In addition, preliminary analysis of the early OL marker breast carcinoma amplified sequence 1 (BCAS1) did not reveal obvious differences between the two genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: EGFP+ oligodendrocyte density did not differ significantly between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice in cortex, corpus callosum, and spinal cord at P28 and P56.
source: Again, we did not detect significant differences in EGFP+ OL density between the two genotypes in three examined CNS regions (CTX, CC, and spinal cord), at two different ages (P28, P56; Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3B and C

claim: The density of NG2+ OL progenitor cells did not differ between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: We also detected no difference in the density of NG2+ OL progenitor cells (OPCs) between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3D and E

claim: There were no differences in the number of newly formed EGFP-labeled ASPA+ oligodendrocytes between control and Zdhhc9 KO mice in OPC fate tracing experiments.
source: However, we did not detect differences in the number of newly formed EGFP-labeled ASPA+ OLs and % of EGFP+ OLs (Figure 3H, I) and the ratio of OLs to OPCs among EGFP-labeled cells (data not shown) between the two groups.
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3H and I

claim: Zdhhc9 KO does not alter oligodendrogenesis in either the young or mature CNS.
source: These results suggest that Zdhhc9 KO does not alter oligodendrogenesis in either the young or mature CNS, at least using the markers and methodologies that we employed.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of differences in OL numbers and fate tracing results

claim: The overall oligodendrocyte process complexity was slightly increased in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: Sholl analysis of these reconstructions revealed that the overall OL process complexity was slightly increased in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis data in Figure 4C

claim: The primary and secondary branch processes were longer in Zdhhc9 KO than control mice.
source: More surprisingly, the primary and secondary branch process were longer in Zdhhc9 KO than control mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by process length quantification in Figure 4D

claim: In control mice, the EGFP-labeled processes originating from one oligodendrocyte soma were of similar thickness, with a uniformly smooth structure.
source: In control mice, the EGFP-labeled processes originating from one OL soma were of similar thickness, with a uniformly smooth structure.
evidence: Based on observation of images in Figure 5A

claim: The thickness of mEGFP+ processes in Zdhhc9 KO mice was far more heterogeneous, with several spheroid-like swellings.
source: However, the thickness of mEGFP+ processes in Zdhhc9 KO mice was far more heterogeneous, with several spheroid-like swellings (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 5A and B

claim: The abnormal spheroid-like swellings on oligodendrocyte processes were distinguished from oligodendrocyte somas as they lack signal for DAPI or Olig2.
source: Notably, the abnormal spheroid-like swellings on OL processes were distinguished from OL somas as they lack signal for DAPI or Olig2 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Zdhhc9 KO oligodendrocytes have significant structural abnormalities in their processes.
source: Careful tracing of EGFP+ OL processes connected to DAPI+ cell body and quantification of spheroid-like swellings devoid of DAPI signal (Figure 5C-1, C-2) revealed significant structural abnormalities in OL processes in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 5D and E

claim: Zdhhc9 loss greatly alters the structure of individual oligodendrocyte processes at the microscopic level.
source: These results indicate that, in contrast to its lack of effect at the gross level, Zdhhc9 loss greatly alters the structure of individual OL processes at the microscopic level, presumably due to abnormal OL membrane expansion.
evidence: Inferred from the structural abnormalities observed in Figure 5

claim: The number of axons did not differ between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice in P56 corpus callosum.
source: In electron micrographs from P56 CC, the number of axons did not differ between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6A and B

claim: Most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice.
source: However, while most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice, myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal; with many large axons unmyelinated (Figure 6A and C) and a subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appearing to be hypermyelinated (Figure 6A and D).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images in Figure 6A

claim: Myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal, with many large axons unmyelinated.
source: However, while most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice, myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal; with many large axons unmyelinated (Figure 6A and C) and a subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appearing to be hypermyelinated (Figure 6A and D).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification in Figure 6A and C

claim: A subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appeared to be hypermyelinated in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: However, while most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice, myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal; with many large axons unmyelinated (Figure 6A and C) and a subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appearing to be hypermyelinated (Figure 6A and D).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification in Figure 6A and D

claim: G-ratios of small diameter axons were smaller in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: Consistent with the latter finding, g-ratios of these small diameter axons were smaller in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Supported by g-ratio analysis in Figure 6E and F

claim: At P30, both hypo- and hypermyelination of axons was already noticeable in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: However, in Zdhhc9 KO mice, both hypo- and hypermyelination of axons was already noticeable at this developmental stage (Figure 6G), which was evident from an increased interquartile range of g-ratios (Figure 6H, I).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and g-ratio analysis in Figure 6G, H, I

claim: Zdhhc9 loss results in dysmyelination.
source: These findings suggest that Zdhhc9 loss results in dysmyelination and, thus, that ZDHHC9 is required for proper initial myelination of individual axons.
evidence: Inferred from the myelination deficits observed at P30 and P56

claim: ZDHHC9 is required for proper initial myelination of individual axons.
source: These findings suggest that Zdhhc9 loss results in dysmyelination and, thus, that ZDHHC9 is required for proper initial myelination of individual axons.
evidence: Inferred from the myelination deficits observed at P30 and P56

claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes had significantly reduced expression of MBP, compared to oligodendrocytes infected to express a scrambled shRNA.
source: Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs had significantly reduced expression of MBP, compared to OLs infected to express a scrambled shRNA (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 7B–D

claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes still expressed CNP, an early myelin-specific protein of developing oligodendrocytes.
source: However, Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs still expressed 2',3'-Cyclic nucleotide 3'-phosphodiesterase (CNP), an early myelin-specific protein of developing OLs (Baumann and Pham-Dinh, 2001; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: ZDHHC9 is not required for initial differentiation of OPCs to oligodendrocytes.
source: This result suggests that ZDHHC9 is not required for initial differentiation of OPCs to OLs, consistent with the normal number of OLs seen in Zdhhc9 KO mice in vivo (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from CNP expression in Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs and normal OL numbers in KO mice

claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes were morphologically immature.
source: However, consistent with the reduced and restricted MBP expression, Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs were also morphologically immature (Figure 7E) with a reduced degree of branching confirmed by Sholl analysis (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and Sholl analysis in Figure 7E and F

claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes had a reduced degree of branching.
source: However, consistent with the reduced and restricted MBP expression, Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs were also morphologically immature (Figure 7E) with a reduced degree of branching confirmed by Sholl analysis (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis in Figure 7F

claim: Zdhhc9 loss cell-autonomously impairs oligodendrocyte maturation in vitro.
source: These data indicate that Zdhhc9 loss cell-autonomously impairs OL maturation in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of acute Zdhhc9 knockdown in cultured OLs

claim: Palmitoylation of 21.5 kDa MBP was very low when transfected alone.
source: Palmitoylation of 21.5 kDa MBP (one of two MBP isoforms that contains a cysteine residue and is thus capable of undergoing palmitoylation) was very low when transfected alone.
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8A and B

claim: MBP palmitoylation remained very low when either HA-ZDHHC9 or myc-Golga7 were co-transfected in isolation.
source: MBP palmitoylation remained very low when either HA-ZDHHC9 or myc-Golga7 were co-transfected in isolation (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8A and B

claim: MBP palmitoylation was greatly increased by co-transfection of HA-ZDHHC9 and myc-Golga7.
source: However, MBP palmitoylation was greatly increased by co-transfection of HA-ZDHHC9 and myc-Golga7 (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8A and B

claim: Zdhhc9 KO did not affect total MBP levels measured by western blotting.
source: Consistent with in vivo immunostaining results (Figure 3A), Zdhhc9 KO did not affect total MBP levels measured by western blotting (all isoforms assessed together; Figure 8C and D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 8C and D

claim: Palmitoylation of both the 17 kDa and 21.5 kDa MBP isoforms was significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: Importantly, palmitoylation, but not total expression, of both the 17 kDa and 21.5 kDa MBP isoforms was significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data from brain tissue in Figure 8C and D

claim: Total and palmitoyl- levels of MAG were significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: Total and palmitoyl- levels of MAG were also significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice, although the palmitoyl:total ratio of MAG was not (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: The palmitoyl:total ratio of MAG was not significantly affected in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: Total and palmitoyl- levels of MAG were also significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice, although the palmitoyl:total ratio of MAG was not (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Neither palmitoyl-, total, nor palmitoyl:total levels of Cadm4 were affected in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
source: In the same samples, neither palmitoyl-, total, nor palmitoyl:total levels of Cadm4 were affected in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: ZDHHC9 directly palmitoylates MBP with the support of Golga7.

claim: Patients with ZDHHC9 mutations have been diagnosed as young as two years of age based on behavioral milestones.

claim: P30 mice are approximately equivalent to a 3-year-old human.

claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice have seizures, reminiscent of the rolandic epilepsy reported in many human patients with ZDHHC9 mutation.
source: Most notably, Zdhhc9 KO mice have seizures, reminiscent of the rolandic epilepsy reported in many human patients with ZDHHC9 mutation (Baker et al., 2015; Shimell et al., 2019).

claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice have impaired latency to reach a hidden platform in the Morris Water Maze.

claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice do not differ significantly in reference memory in a probe trial.
source: However, the KO mice do not differ significantly in reference memory in a subsequent probe trial, suggesting that, despite the increased latency, they do learn the location of the platform as effectively as wt (Kouskou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice have decreased levels of anxiety.
source: In addition, performance in both the open field and in an elevated plus maze (EPM, in which the KO mice spend significantly more time in the open arms) suggests that Zdhhc9 KO mice also have decreased levels of anxiety (Kouskou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Decreased anxiety is reported in several other mouse models of intellectual disability.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Impaired palmitoylation of MBP, and potentially other myelin proteins, in the absence of ZDHHC9 affects myelin structure.

evidence: Speculative inference based on known role of palmitoylation and observed myelin deficits

claim: ZDHHC9 may act at Golgi outposts to drive the expression of myelin protein genes.

claim: The association with Golga7 is central to ZDHHC9 activity.
source: Interestingly, despite their marked differences in basal catalytic activity (as assessed by autopalmitoylation), wt and all XLID forms of ZDHHC9 appear to show enhanced activity (measured by both auto- and MBP palmitoylation) in the presence of Golga7, suggesting that the association with Golga7 (which also localizes to Golgi outposts) is central to ZDHHC9 activity.
evidence: Inferred from the enhancement of ZDHHC9 activity by Golga7 in ABE assays

claim: Oligodendrocyte and white matter abnormalities could significantly contribute to ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
source: Together, though, our findings suggest that OL and WM abnormalities could significantly contribute to ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
evidence: Inferred from the OL and myelin deficits observed in Zdhhc9 KO mice

claim: Impaired subcellular localization in oligodendrocytes, rather than impaired catalytic activity, may cause or contribute to white matter abnormalities in some cases of ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
source: Interestingly, the XLID mutant ZDHHC9-P150S still palmitoylates MBP in a Golga7-dependent manner in transfected non-neuronal cells, raising the possibility that impaired subcellular localization in OLs, rather than impaired catalytic activity, may cause or contribute to WM abnormalities in some cases of ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the retained catalytic activity but impaired localization of ZDHHC9-P150S
